lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Common practice treats the leads of an event study as a test: if none is significantly different from zero, assume parallel trends and move on. <bookmark mark='b'/> Jonathan Roth showed in 2022 that these pre-tests often have little power against violations large enough to matter. <bookmark mark='c'/> Worse, reporting only the studies that pass them distorts what gets reported, Part thirty-three's selection again. <bookmark mark='d'/> The better approach is to say how far from parallel the trends might plausibly be, and carry that uncertainty into the conclusion.
lines.spoken: Common practice treats the leads of an event study as a test: if none is significantly different from zero, assume parallel trends and move on. Jonathan Roth showed in 2022 that these pre-tests often have little power against violations large enough to matter. Worse, reporting only the studies that pass them distorts what gets reported, Part thirty-three's selection again. The better approach is to say how far from parallel the trends might plausibly be, and carry that uncertainty into the conclusion.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> A seeded example, with a hundred and fifty towns that adopt a programme in 2010, chosen because they were already improving, and a hundred and fifty that never adopt. <bookmark mark='b'/> Their untreated employment rises two tenths of a point a year faster. The leads show it: a steady climb towards zero. <bookmark mark='c'/> The programme adds exactly one point from adoption on. <bookmark mark='d'/> But the first-year estimate is one point one seven, and the lags keep climbing, because the pre-existing trend is read as effect. The conventional interval excludes the truth.
lines.spoken: A seeded example, with a hundred and fifty towns that adopt a programme in 2010, chosen because they were already improving, and a hundred and fifty that never adopt. Their untreated employment rises two tenths of a point a year faster. The leads show it: a steady climb towards zero. The programme adds exactly one point from adoption on. But the first-year estimate is one point one seven, and the lags keep climbing, because the pre-existing trend is read as effect. The conventional interval excludes the truth.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Ashesh Rambachan and Jonathan Roth's framework, published in 2023, writes the population event-study coefficient as the effect plus the violation of parallel trends. Estimates add sampling error, correlated across event times. <bookmark mark='b'/> Before adoption there is no effect, so the leads estimate the violation directly. <bookmark mark='c'/> Then they restrict how the violation may continue after adoption. Our simplified first-post-period model bounds departure from a fitted population linear pre-trend by M. It illustrates sensitivity but differs from their full smoothness-restriction procedure. <bookmark mark='d'/> Under relative magnitudes, the jump after adoption is at most M-bar times the largest jump seen before it. We account for the full joint covariance in the linear extrapolation, and use simultaneous pre-jump bounds for the relative-magnitude interval. These are asymptotic intervals under the stated teaching restrictions.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> For the first year after adoption. On the left, in red, the conventional interval, which misses the truth. <bookmark mark='b'/> With M equal to zero, the violation is assumed to continue the linear pre-trend exactly. Subtracting it gives point nine seven, with an interval that covers the truth of one. <bookmark mark='c'/> Allowing the trend to bend by up to M widens the set, in gold, and its interval, in green. <bookmark mark='d'/> The conclusion that the programme helped survives until M is about point eight seven, a departure from this particular linear extrapolation. Its scale and interpretation depend on the restriction being imposed. That breakdown value is what a reader needs in order to judge.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Under relative magnitudes, the largest year-to-year change in the leads is point three zero. <bookmark mark='b'/> If the violation can jump after adoption by half that, or by as much, the effect is clearly positive. <bookmark mark='c'/> Even if it can jump by twice the largest change seen before, the interval stays above zero, from point one one. The post-treatment restrictions cannot be verified from pre-treatment outcomes alone; the point is to make the assumption explicit, and to let a reader with a different view recompute the answer.

lines.raw: <bookmark mark='a'/> Parallel trends is an assumption about what would have happened. The leads inform it; they cannot prove it. <bookmark mark='b'/> So report the event study, the sensitivity sets, and the breakdown value, the departure at which the conclusion changes. <bookmark mark='c'/> It is the same spirit as the E-values and robustness values of Part thirty-six. <bookmark mark='d'/> Next: what to do when only one unit was treated, and there are many possible controls.
